message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
This proposal is built on our own trading history, not just competitor benchmarking, and that is what makes me confident in it. The key question with any rate rise is price sensitivity, and we have a direct test: when we raised the weekend rate by £10 last June, weekend occupancy went up, from 81% to 89%, the following month. Combined with a value-for-money score of 8.4, the best in our set, and rates £20 to £35 below competitors, everything points the same way. The revenue estimate is deliberately conservative: it assumes no occupancy gain and puts no value at all on the extra Friday and Sunday nights that the two-night minimum will generate, so £204,000 is a floor rather than a target. We have also built in a clear monitoring trigger, so if occupancy does dip we will see it within a month and can respond. Corporate and group commitments are protected. I think this is a well-evidenced, low-risk change that brings our pricing into line with the quality of the hotel.
</author>

<document>
Pricing Proposal: Weekend Rate Restructure
Harbourside Hotel, Revenue Management, April 2026

1. Proposal
From 1 June 2026 we propose to (a) raise the Best Available Rate (BAR) for Friday and Saturday nights from £145 to £165, and (b) introduce a two-night minimum for any stay that includes a Saturday night. Midweek rates are unchanged.

2. Context
Harbourside is a 112-room four-star hotel on the quay, with a leisure-led weekend business and a corporate-led midweek business. Our weekend BAR is £20 to £35 below the three comparable hotels in our competitive set, whose weekend rates currently range from £165 to £180. Weekend occupancy has recovered strongly since 2023 and we believe we are leaving money on the table.

Table 1. Weekend (Friday and Saturday) occupancy by month, 2025
Jan 62% | Feb 66% | Mar 74% | Apr 80% | May 85% | Jun 81%
Jul 89% | Aug 93% | Sep 88% | Oct 82% | Nov 72% | Dec 78%

Average weekend occupancy across 2025 was 79%. July and August are our strongest months, driven by the harbour festival and the school summer holidays, with September also benefiting from late-season visitors.

3. Evidence on price sensitivity
In the last week of June 2025 we raised the weekend BAR by £10, from £135 to the current £145. Weekend occupancy in July rose to 89%, from 81% in June. This tells us that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current levels; if anything, the higher rate appears to have reinforced our positioning as a quality option, and we expect the further increase to be absorbed in the same way.

This is consistent with feedback from our guest satisfaction surveys, where weekend guests rate "value for money" at 8.4 out of 10, the highest score among our competitive set.

4. Two-night minimum
Saturday nights are our most constrained inventory: we sold out on 31 Saturdays in 2025. Many of these guests stay only one night, leaving rooms empty on Friday or Sunday either side. A two-night minimum for stays including a Saturday will convert single-night Saturday stays into two-night stays and smooth occupancy across the weekend.

Our booking data show that weddings at Quayside Hall, the venue next door, account for around 38% of our Saturday-night room bookings. Wedding guests typically book as a block through the couple, arrive on the Saturday afternoon and check out on the Sunday morning.

5. Revenue impact
Across our 124 rooms, 104 weekend nights a year and average weekend occupancy of 79%, a £20 increase in BAR is worth about £204,000 a year in additional room revenue, before any gain from longer stays. We have assumed weekend occupancy is maintained at 2025 levels, which we consider prudent given the evidence above.

The two-night minimum should add further revenue through additional Friday and Sunday nights. We have not quantified this but expect it to be material, particularly in shoulder months.

6. Implementation and monitoring
The new rates will be loaded into the channel manager on 15 May for stays from 1 June, giving online travel agencies two weeks' notice. Corporate contracted rates and group rates already contracted will be honoured. We will review pick-up weekly against the same weeks in 2025 and report to the General Manager monthly. If weekend occupancy for any month falls more than five points below 2025, we will review the rate.

7. Recommendation
The evidence shows that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current rates and that we are priced well below our competitive set. We recommend approval of the £165 weekend BAR and the two-night Saturday minimum from 1 June 2026, delivering at least £204,000 of additional annual room revenue.
</document>
response:
The case for raising the weekend rate may well be right: the hotel is priced well below its competitors and sells out most Saturdays. But the proposal's evidence doesn't support its confidence:
- The price-sensitivity "test" is confounded by the summer season.
- The revenue figure uses the wrong number of rooms and overstates the gain in other ways, so it is not a floor.
- The two-night minimum could reduce revenue, especially among the wedding guests who make up 38% of Saturday bookings.

## 1. The June-to-July "test" measures the season, not price

Occupancy rose from 81% in June to 89% in July after the £10 rise. But the paper itself says July and August are the strongest months because of the harbour festival and school holidays. Occupancy would have risen in July with or without the price change.

The proper comparison is July 2025 against July 2024, and against the June-to-July change in earlier years. If July normally runs 10 points above June, an 8-point rise means the price increase *cost* about 2 points.

The value-for-money score of 8.4 doesn't settle it either:
- It was measured at the old, lower prices. Guests may rate value highly partly *because* the hotel is £20–35 cheaper than its competitors.
- It comes from people who booked, and says nothing about the guests a higher price would lose.

## 2. The £204,000 is an overestimate, not a floor

**The room count is wrong.** Section 2 says 112 rooms, but section 5 uses 124. With 112 rooms:

> 112 rooms × 104 nights × 79% × £20 ≈ **£184,000**, not £204,000.

**It assumes every occupied weekend room pays BAR.** BAR is the hotel's standard public rate, and many weekend rooms don't pay it:
- **Weddings:** the paper says wedding guests book "as a block through the couple", which means a group rate. They are 38% of Saturday bookings.
- **Other non-BAR rooms:** corporate rates, packages and discounted channels.

The £20 increase applies only to rooms actually sold at BAR. If, for example, 60% of weekend room-nights are sold at BAR, the gain falls to about £110,000. The real share is in the booking system and should be used.

**It's gross of commission.** Rooms sold through online travel agencies lose 15–20% of the rate to commission.

**The first year is partial.** Summer weekends will be heavily booked at the old rate by 15 May, when the new rates load.

**Holding occupancy at 2025 levels is not a cautious assumption.** It is the central assumption behind the whole figure, and section 1 gives no evidence for it.

## 3. The two-night minimum could reduce revenue

**It conflicts with the wedding business.** Wedding guests arrive Saturday and leave Sunday, and they are 38% of Saturday bookings. The proposal protects only group rates *already contracted*. Future wedding blocks would either need an exemption, or would lose guests to other hotels near the venue next door. Either way, the minimum won't turn those guests into two-night stays.

**It helps on sold-out Saturdays and costs bookings on the rest.**
- On the 31 sold-out Saturdays, requiring two nights can replace one-night guests with two-night guests, which adds revenue.
- On the other 21 Saturdays, and across the quieter spring and autumn months, it turns away one-night guests who would otherwise have filled empty rooms.

The paper expects the benefit "particularly in shoulder months". That gets it the wrong way round: shoulder months are where the minimum is most likely to cost money.

**The two changes compound.** A guest who wanted one Saturday night used to pay £145. They would now have to pay at least £330 for two nights, more than double. The paper treats the price rise and the minimum stay separately, but guests experience them together.

Because the minimum can cost bookings, leaving it unquantified is not conservative. Its effect could be negative, and it works against the assumption that occupancy holds.

## 4. The monitoring trigger is too slow

Pick-up (new bookings received) is reviewed weekly, but the trigger is a full month's occupancy falling more than five points below 2025. By the time a month has finished and been reported, the following months are already partly booked at the new terms.

The trigger should be based on booking pace instead: forward bookings for future weekends compared with the same point last year. Set a threshold that is checked weekly.

For reference, ignoring the share of rooms not sold at BAR, room revenue breaks even at about 69% occupancy, roughly 10 points below 2025. The five-point trigger is therefore reasonable in size, but it should also account for food, drink and other spending lost with each guest who goes elsewhere.

## 5. Smaller points

- **Positioning.** At £165 the hotel would match the cheapest competitor, not undercut it. That may be justified by quality, but the price advantage would be gone.
- **Recovery since 2023.** The paper says occupancy "has recovered strongly since 2023" but shows no figures for that period.

## How the claims compare with the document

| Claim | What the document shows |
|---|---|
| "A direct test" of price sensitivity | A seasonal rise that coincided with a price change |
| "Assumes no occupancy gain"; "£204,000 is a floor" | Uses 124 rooms instead of 112, assumes all rooms at BAR, ignores commission |
| "No value on the extra nights", so conservative | The minimum stay could reduce revenue |
| "We will see it within a month" | Only after the month ends |
| "Corporate and group commitments are protected" | Only those already contracted; future wedding blocks aren't addressed |

## Suggested revisions

1. **Replace the June-to-July evidence** with year-on-year comparisons. Better still, run a controlled test, for example raising the rate only on selected weekends or in selected channels.
2. **Recalculate revenue** with 112 rooms, using the actual share of rooms sold at BAR, net of commission, and pro-rated for the first year.
3. **Limit the two-night minimum** to Saturdays forecast to sell out, and exempt wedding and other group blocks. Estimate its effect on displaced one-night bookings.
4. **Change the trigger** to a weekly booking-pace check against last year.
5. **Consider phasing the increase**, for example £155 first, since the June evidence can't tell you how sensitive guests are to price.
